شريط الأخبار عناوين الأخبار الأمم المتحدة: مقتل 2230 مدنياً خلال 10 أشهر جراء حرب السودان 17/11/2026 12:58 أحد أفراد حفظ السلام في قوة الأمم المتحدة الأمنية المؤقتة لأبيي يقف في موقع هجمات بطائرات مسيرة أدت إلى مقتل وإصابة الكثيرين. المصدر :UNIFSA أمستردام – 17 نوفمبر 2026 – راديو دبنقا كشف مكتب الأمم المتحدة لحقوق الإنسان عن مقتل ما لا يقل عن 2230 مدنياً خلال الفترة من يناير إلى أكتوبر، من بينهم أكثر من 1630 شخصاً جراء هجمات الطائرات المسيّرة. وأكد التقرير، الذي صدر اليوم الثلاثاء، أن أكثر من 1390 مدنياً قُتلوا في النزاع الدائر بين القوات المسلحة السودانية وقوات الدعم السريع والحركات المسلحة المتحالفة معهما، وذلك خلال الفترة من يناير إلى يونيو من العام الحالي. وأشار التقرير إلى أن أكثر من 80 في المائة من هؤلاء الضحايا سقطوا جراء غارات شنتها طائرات مسيّرة، باتت تشكل «سمة مميزة» لهذه الحرب. وخلال الأشهر الأربعة التالية، قُتل 840 مدنياً إضافياً، من بينهم نحو 520 شخصاً لقوا حتفهم جراء غارات الطائرات المسيّرة. وأوضح التقرير أن هذه الأرقام تمثل الحالات التي تمكن مكتب الأمم المتحدة لحقوق الإنسان من التحقق منها، في حين يُرجح أن تكون الأعداد الفعلية للضحايا المدنيين أعلى من ذلك. وخلص التقرير إلى أن التجاهل المستمر لواجب حماية المدنيين يواصل تكبيد الشعب السوداني «خسائر لا تُطاق». استهداف المدنيين والأعيان المدنية ويوثق التقرير، الذي يغطي النصف الأول من عام 2026، اتجاهات وأنماطاً ظلت ثابتة طوال فترة النزاع، بما في ذلك استهداف المدنيين والأعيان المدنية، وشن هجمات عشوائية، وتنفيذ أعمال انتقامية ضد مدنيين يُتهمون بـ«التعاون» مع القوات المناوئة، فضلاً عن استمرار استخدام العنف الجنسي سلاحاً في الحرب. كما يثير التقرير مخاوف بشأن استمرار عمليات القتل غير القانوني والاحتجاز التعسفي وتقلص الحيز المدني. ويذكر التقرير أنه خلال الفترة المشمولة بالرصد، «تغيرت خطوط المواجهة وتطورت التكتيكات العسكرية، لا سيما استخدام الطائرات المسيّرة، لكن الخسائر الفادحة التي يتكبدها الشعب السوداني جراء الحرب ظلت ثابتة كما كانت دائماً، في ظل تجاهل صارخ لحماية المدنيين». أدلة إضافية وقال مفوض الأمم المتحدة السامي لحقوق الإنسان، فولكر تورك: «الحقائق تتحدث عن نفسها. فما توصل إليه تقريرنا يقدم أدلة إضافية، إن كانت هناك حاجة إلى مزيد من الأدلة، على المعاناة المدنية التي لا تُطاق جراء الحرب الدائرة في السودان، وعلى استمرار الأطراف المتحاربة في تجاهلها الصارخ لقوانين الحرب». وأضاف: «في ظل تفشي الإفلات من العقاب، يوثق التقرير، مرة أخرى، انتهاكات جسيمة للقانون الدولي الإنساني، وهي انتهاكات قد ترقى إلى مستوى جرائم الحرب». وكان المدنيون في منطقة كردفان الأكثر تضرراً، إذ شكلوا أكثر من ثلثي الضحايا المدنيين الموثقين، تلتهم منطقة دارفور التي شهدت وقوع معظم الضحايا المتبقين. كما تأثرت المناطق الشرقية والوسطى من السودان بهجمات الطائرات المسيّرة، ولا سيما ولاية النيل الأبيض، التي قُتل فيها ما لا يقل عن 41 مدنياً خلال الفترة التي يغطيها التقرير. وقد تعرضت أسواق ومستشفيات ومدارس ومرافق إمداد بالوقود ومصادر مياه ومواقع للنازحين ومركبات مدنية للقصف، حيث استُهدفت بعض هذه المواقع بشكل متكرر. 39 غارة بطائرة مسيّرة وفي النصف الأول من عام 2026، وثّق مكتب الأمم المتحدة لحقوق الإنسان ما لا يقل عن 39 غارة بطائرات مسيّرة استهدفت أسواقاً، و20 غارة استهدفت مركبات مدنية، و17 غارة استهدفت صهاريج ومستودعات وقود، و16 غارة استهدفت مرافق صحية. وتثير هذه الهجمات مخاوف جدية بشأن مدى الامتثال لقواعد الحرب التي تحمي المدنيين والأعيان المدنية، بما في ذلك الأعيان التي لا غنى عنها لبقاء السكان المدنيين على قيد الحياة، وكذلك بشأن حماية العاملين في القطاع الصحي والمرافق الصحية، لا سيما في مناطق هي في أمس الحاجة بالفعل إلى المساعدات الإنسانية والطبية. ويشير التقرير إلى أن الهجمات بالطائرات المسيّرة على الأسواق، إلى جانب أعمال النهب والقيود المفروضة على التنقل، أعاقت بشدة إمكانية الحصول على الغذاء. وفي أكتوبر/تشرين الأول، حذرت «المبادرة العالمية للتصنيف المرحلي المتكامل للأمن الغذائي» (IPC) من أن النزاع والنزوح والجفاف تؤدي إلى تزايد خطر حدوث مجاعة في أجزاء من دارفور وكردفان، في ظل ارتفاع مستويات انعدام الأمن الغذائي الحاد وسوء التغذية. وقد سُجل عدد كبير من الضحايا في شهر أكتوبر، الذي شهد أيضاً تصاعداً في الهجمات بالطائرات المسيّرة ضد الأعيان المدنية، مما خلّف آثاراً مدمرة على السكان المدنيين. اتجاهات مقلقة ومن بين الاتجاهات المقلقة، التصعيد الأخير للهجمات بالطائرات المسيّرة التي تستهدف محطات توليد الطاقة وإمدادات الوقود. ففي غضون ما يزيد قليلاً على أسبوعين، وتحديداً خلال الفترة من 20 أكتوبر/تشرين الأول إلى 4 نوفمبر/تشرين الثاني، وقعت 29 غارة بطائرات مسيّرة، نُسبت إلى قوات الدعم السريع، استهدفت مرافق كهربائية ومحطات وقود في 11 ولاية، مما تسبب في انقطاعات واسعة النطاق للتيار الكهربائي وتفاقم نقص الوقود، وهو ما أثر على ملايين الأشخاص بعيداً عن خطوط المواجهة. وكان لهذه الهجمات أثر مدمر على المدنيين والخدمات الأساسية؛ إذ تسببت في انقطاع الكهرباء، مما أدى إلى تعطل الخدمات الصحية، بما في ذلك عمليات غسيل الكلى والجراحات، فضلاً عن عرقلة الوصول إلى المياه النظيفة وإنتاج الغذاء. ويضيف التقرير أن المساءلة، بغض النظر عن انتماء الجناة، تُعد أمراً جوهرياً لكسر دوائر العنف ومنع وقوع المزيد من الانتهاكات والتجاوزات. وشدد المفوض السامي تورك على ضرورة أن تعمل أطراف النزاع على حماية المدنيين والوفاء بالتزاماتها بموجب القانون الدولي، مؤكداً أن «العالم يراقب». sudan.summary: كشف مكتب الأمم المتحدة لحقوق الإنسان عن مقتل 2230 مدنياً في السودان خلال عشرة أشهر من النزاع، بين يناير وأكتوبر 2026. من بين هؤلاء، قُتل أكثر من 1630 شخصاً نتيجة هجمات الطائرات المسيّرة، التي أصبحت سمة بارزة في الصراع بين القوات المسلحة السودانية وقوات الدعم السريع. التقرير أشار إلى أن 80% من الضحايا سقطوا جراء الغارات الجوية، مع تسجيل 1390 قتيلاً في النصف الأول من العام. كما وثق التقرير انتهاكات جسيمة للقانون الدولي، بما في ذلك استهداف المدنيين والأعيان المدنية، مما أدى إلى تفاقم الأوضاع الإنسانية. المناطق الأكثر تضرراً كانت كردفان ودارفور، حيث تعرضت الأسواق والمرافق الصحية للقصف. المفوض السامي لحقوق الإنسان، فولكر تورك، أكد على ضرورة حماية المدنيين والامتثال للقوانين الدولية، محذراً من أن الأرقام قد تكون أعلى من الموثقة.

sudan.content: الانتقال إلى المحتوى الرئيسي Reporting the Changing World وكالتنا لمحة عن تاريخ الوكالة التوصيف الوظيفي نظام إدارة الجودة مبادئ-النشر السياسات-الخاصة-بالإعلام-الاجتماعي سياسة الخصوصية والكوكيز سياسة الإفصاح RSS التواصل بيانات الاتصال طلبات الاشتراك Anadolu Ajansı © 2026 تركيا الدول العربية دولي اقتصاد رياضة تقارير كوب 31 أنطاليا 3 سنوات من الإبادة الاعتداءات في الضفة الغربية EDITION Türkçe English BHSC Pусский Français العربية Kurdî کوردی Shqip فارسی македонски Bahasa Indonesia Español السودان السودان.. نزوح 400 شخص إضافي من مدينة أبو زبد خلال يومين ليرتفع عدد النازحين من المدينة بولاية غرب كردفان إلى 1150 شخصا خلال 3 أيام، وفق بيانات المنظمة الدولية للهجرة.. Adel Abdelrheem 17 نوفمبر 2026 • تحديث : 17 نوفمبر 2026 SUDAN السودان/ عادل عبد الرحيم/ الأناضول أعلنت المنظمة الدولية للهجرة، الثلاثاء، نزوح 400 شخص إضافي من مدينة أبو زبد بولاية غرب كردفان جنوبي السودان، خلال يومين، جراء انعدام الأمن، ليرتفع إجمالي النازحين منها إلى 1150 شخصا خلال 3 أيام. وأفادت المنظمة، في بيان، بأن فرقها الميدانية لرصد النزوح قدّرت نزوح 400 شخصا إضافيا من مدينة أبو زبد بولاية غرب كردفان، نتيجة تفاقم انعدام الأمن خلال يومي 15 و16 نوفمبر/تشرين الثاني الجاري. وأوضحت أن النازحين توجهوا إلى محافظات كيلك والسنط والسلام والقوة في ولاية غرب كردفان. وأكدت أن الوضع لا يزال متوترا ومتقلبا للغاية، وأنها تراقب الأوضاع عن قرب. وأضافت أن موجة النزوح الجديدة تأتي عقب حوادث مماثلة شهدتها المنطقة في 14 نوفمبر الجاري. وفي ذلك اليوم، أعلنت المنظمة الدولية للهجرة، في بيان، نزوح 750 شخصا من مدينة أبو زبد، خلال يوم واحد، جراء انعدام الأمن. ومنذ أيام، تشهد ولاية غرب كردفان تصاعدا في المواجهات العسكرية بين الجيش السوداني وقوات الدعم السريع. وتتفاقم المعاناة الإنسانية في السودان جراء الحرب بين الجيش وقوات الدعم السريع، المستمرة منذ أبريل/ نيسان 2023، بسبب خلاف بشأن توحيد المؤسسة العسكرية، ما أسفر عن مقتل عشرات الآلاف ونزوح نحو 13 مليون شخص. news_share news_share_description subscription_contact subscription contact_the_ombudsman is_there_an_error_in_this_story ombudsman_apply_button السودان.. نزوح 400 شخص إضافي من مدينة أبو زبد خلال يومين أحدث الأخبار الكل من هو متان كاهانا.. الرئيس الجديد للكنيست الإسرائيلي؟ مسؤول إيراني: لا أضرار جراء الهجوم الأمريكي على جزيرة قشم وفد أكاديمي تركي يبحث في لبنان تعزيز التعاون الجامعي وتبادل الخبرات إيران تعلن احتراق ناقلة نفط رابعة في مضيق هرمز متان كاهانا رئيسا للكنيست الإسرائيلي وخسارة مرشح الليكود عون: نعمل على بناء الثقة مع المجتمع الدولي ونعول على دور عربي أكبر قائد "سنتكوم" يزور إسرائيل ويلتقي رئيس الأركان وقادة بالجيش عرض الكل السابق السابق الأمم المتحدة: المسيّرات قتلت أكثر من 1630 مدنيا بالسودان في 10 شهور
sudan.summary: أعلنت المنظمة الدولية للهجرة عن نزوح 400 شخص إضافي من مدينة أبو زبد في ولاية غرب كردفان، مما يرفع إجمالي النازحين من المدينة إلى 1150 شخصًا خلال ثلاثة أيام. جاء هذا النزوح نتيجة لتفاقم انعدام الأمن في المنطقة، حيث تم تسجيل هذه الحوادث خلال يومي 15 و16 نوفمبر. النازحون توجهوا إلى محافظات كيلك والسنط والسلام والقوة. الوضع في غرب كردفان لا يزال متوترًا، مع استمرار المواجهات العسكرية بين الجيش السوداني وقوات الدعم السريع، مما يزيد من معاناة السكان. منذ بداية النزاع في أبريل 2023، قُتل عشرات الآلاف ونزح حوالي 13 مليون شخص. المنظمة الدولية للهجرة تراقب الوضع عن كثب، حيث شهدت المنطقة موجات نزوح متكررة، بما في ذلك نزوح 750 شخصًا في يوم واحد في 14 نوفمبر.

ethiopia.title: Stationing of Ethiopian Peacekeepers over 7 Decades Reflects Commitment to Collective Security: IPSTI - ENA English
ethiopia.content: Stationing of Ethiopian Peacekeepers over 7 Decades Reflects Commitment to Collective Security: IPSTI - ENA English - ENA Skip to Content Stationing of Ethiopian Peacekeepers over 7 Decades Reflects Commitment to Collective Security: IPSTI - ENA English Live: አማርኛ ትግርኛ Afaan Oromoo Af‑Soomaali Qafar Afa English Français عربي Politics Social Economy Sport Technology Environment Feature Videos About Us Stationing of Ethiopian Peacekeepers over 7 Decades Reflects Commitment to Collective Security: IPSTI 🔇Unmute Addis Ababa, November 17, 2026 (ENA)— Ethiopia's deployment of peacekeepers over the last seven decades reflects its longstanding commitment to collective security, regional stability and international cooperation, Brigadier General Gezahegn Fekadu, Ethiopian National Defense Force International Peace Support Training Institute (IPSTI) Commandant said. The country’s peacekeeping engagement began with the Korean War and continued through missions in countries including Sudan, South Sudan and Somalia, demonstrating its sustained involvement in international and regional peace efforts, he added. The Commandant made the remarks at a consultative forum organized jointly by IPSTI and the Ethiopian National Defense College to examine strategies for sustaining Ethiopia’s peacekeeping role amid changing global dynamics. Brigadier General Gezahegn said the evolving global order, declining funding for peace operations and political disagreements among multilateral institutions are creating challenges for countries contributing to international peacekeeping, including Ethiopia. As a major troop-contributing country, Ethiopia therefore needs to strengthen its operational readiness, modernize its capabilities and develop sustainable partnerships to maintain its contribution to global peace and security, the Commandant noted. The forum examined Ethiopia’s historical peacekeeping contributions, the effects of global and regional transitions, funding and partnership challenges, as well as the country’s operational readiness and future strategy. For his part, Ethiopian National Defense College representative Seraw Demas said Ethiopia’s contribution to regional stability extends beyond peacekeeping deployments. The country also hosts hundreds of thousands of refugees, particularly from neighboring countries, he added. Commandant Seraw noted that Ethiopia has continued to shoulder this humanitarian responsibility despite economic, social and institutional pressures, which have been compounded by constraints in international support, particularly in recent years. Beyond these country-specific considerations, the French Defense Attaché Colonel Damien Cypryk highlighted broader challenges confronting international peacekeeping, saying the changing nature of armed conflicts, driven by the growing use of cyberattacks, information warfare, artificial intelligence and drones, is making operations more complex and demanding new approaches to maintaining international peace and security. Divisions among UN member states over peacekeeping mandates and objectives, alongside growing mistrust among host countries and local communities, are also weakening the effectiveness of missions and making it harder to achieve lasting political solutions. Colonel Cypryk further said the UN peacekeeping system faces serious financial constraints, with liquidity shortages, payment arrears and declining voluntary contributions forcing the closure or downsizing of some missions, sometimes without sufficient consideration of security conditions on the ground. The attaché emphasized that UN peacekeeping operations remain vital to protecting civilians, monitoring ceasefires and supporting peace processes, stressing the need to adapt their mandates, resources and funding to evolving geopolitical, security and operational realities. © Ethiopian News Agency 2023 Hidden

At a recent forum, Gezahegn highlighted challenges such as declining funding for peace operations and political disagreements among multilateral institutions, which affect Ethiopia's role as a major troop contributor. The forum also addressed Ethiopia's historical contributions, operational readiness, and the need for modernization and sustainable partnerships. Additionally, the Ethiopian National Defense College representative noted the country's humanitarian efforts, hosting numerous refugees despite economic pressures. French Defense Attaché Colonel Damien Cypryk emphasized the evolving complexities of peacekeeping, including cyber threats and funding constraints, which necessitate adaptive strategies for effective international peace and security operations. ethiopia.content: Study Finds Remittances Reduced Food Security Among Ethiopian HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER Wednesday, November 18, 2026 No Result View All Result Login HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER No Result View All Result No Result View All Result Home NEWS Science News Agriculture Study Finds Remittances Reduced Food Security Among Ethiopian Agro-Pastoralists by November 17, 2026 in Agriculture Reading Time: 2 mins read 0 Study Finds Remittances Reduced Food Security Among Ethiopian Agro-Pastoralists Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Share on Linkedin Share on Reddit Share on Telegram A new research study examining agro-pastoralists in Lare District, located within the Nuer Zone of the Gambella Region in South-West Ethiopia, found that remittances reduced the food security of recipient households by 0.4267 units compared to non-recipients. Although remittances serve as an important source of financial support for pastoralist households in developing nations facing economic and environmental strain, the study found that remittances reduced the food security of recipient households compared to non-recipients. The investigation employed a mixed-methods design to evaluate the effects of remittances across local agro-pastoralist communities. The authors gathered field data directly from 384 respondents through a comprehensive questionnaire survey and conducted key informant interviews across the district. To evaluate the collected dataset, the researchers utilized a range of statistical procedures, calculating frequency distributions, percentages, arithmetic means, and standard deviations. Survey measurements indicated that 46.6 percent of the respondents in Lare District had received remittances, whereas 53.39 percent of the surveyed households had not received any remittance support. The model estimates established that receiving remittances reduced food security by 0.4267 units among remittance users compared to non-users, confirming an adverse impact on household food security status in the study area. The empirical results further demonstrated that different underlying variables influenced food security depending on whether households received remittances. Among remittance users, food security was significantly influenced by livestock holding size, cultivated land size, distance to water, sex, marital status, and livestock disease. Conversely, the educational level of the respondent influenced the food security outcomes of non-remittance users. In light of these findings, the study highlights the necessity of formulating targeted policies that construct productive investments in remittances while promoting sustainable food security strategies for agro-pastoralist populations in the district. ethiopia.title: Africans Must Reclaim Cultural Narratives - Nebiyou
ethiopia.content: Ethiopia: Africans Must Reclaim Cultural Narratives - Nebiyou - allAfrica.com AllAfrica English (current) En Français Toggle navigation My Account Toggle navigation AllAfrica My Account English (current) En Français Ethiopia: Africans Must Reclaim Cultural Narratives - Nebiyou 17 November 2026 Ethiopian News Agency (Addis Ababa) Addis Ababa — African scholars and institutions should take greater ownership of the study, interpretation and promotion of the continent's cultural heritage, Ethiopia's State Minister for Culture and Tourism, Nebiyou Baye has said. aIn an interview with the Pulse of Africa, Nebiyou emphasized that Africans must tell their own stories to reshape how the world sees the continent. He argued that African cultures have long been examined largely through foreign perspectives, some of which have portrayed the continent's traditions as inferior or backward. He said African researchers, anthropologists and sociologists should take the lead in documenting and interpreting the continent's cultural wealth, adding that a stronger understanding of African heritage is essential to promoting it internationally. Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn "So, primarily, what we have to do is that we have to start studying our culture by ourselves. African anthropologists, African sociologists, African cultural scientists, and African leaders in general, scholars in particular, should be in the front seat in any discussion about African cultural heritages," Nebiyou said. "So, it's when we know what we have that we will be able to promote that endowment to the world." He also stressed the importance of strengthening cultural exchanges among African countries, arguing that the continent should build greater familiarity with its diverse traditions before seeking wider global recognition. The official, who is one of the most recognizable figures in Ethiopia's theatre and cinematic industry, cited Ethiopian cuisine, music, traditional clothing and festivals as cultural assets that could be shared more widely across Africa, encouraging countries to create opportunities for their people to experience one another's cultural expressions. Said Nebiyou: "You know, before we go global, in my view, we have to go African. Do you know, for instance, how many Africans were able to taste kitfo? Let alone how many Africans, our neighbors, for instance. Neighbors from Kenya, Sudan, Djibouti. How many of our neighbors were able to taste, let's just say, injera? So, we need first to reach out to our African brothers and sisters." The State Minister further identified music, cinema and other creative industries as powerful instruments of cultural diplomacy and soft power, pointing to the international reach of West African music, Ethiopian jazz and traditional Eskista dance. A longtime actor and writer himself, Nebiyu previously taught in the School of Theatre Arts at Addis Ababa University as an Assistant Professor. He also served as director of the Ethiopian National Theatre before moving into government. He said African artists and filmmakers have demonstrated how the continent can communicate its identity and experiences through original creative expression. "So that now, those African artists, African creative people, they have showed us a way to follow, a method to emulate, and then become world-class artists. And in a way, in doing that, we'll be able to tell our stories, to promote our culture, to show the world who we are. The world would know that this is Africa," the Master of Arts holder said. ethiopia.title: U.S. Backs One-Year Renewal of UN, AU Security Missions in Somalia After Reversal
ethiopia.content: Somalia: U.S. Backs One-Year Renewal of UN, AU Security Missions in Somalia After Reversal - allAfrica.com AllAfrica English (current) En Français Toggle navigation My Account Toggle navigation AllAfrica My Account English (current) En Français Somalia: U.S. Backs One-Year Renewal of UN, AU Security Missions in Somalia After Reversal 17 November 2026 Addis Standard (Addis Ababa) Addis Abeba — The United States has reversed its earlier position and agreed to support a one-year renewal of the mandates of the UN Support Office in Somalia (UNSOS) and the African Union Support and Stabilisation Mission in Somalia (AUSSOM), offering a reprieve to the AU-led force battling al-Shabaab. A US State Department spokesperson told AFP that Washington would "support a one-year renewal of the mandates" following a review of the security implications of withdrawing support. The spokesperson said the decision was intended to help contain threats emanating from Somalia and "prevent the emergence of broader security crisis in the region that would undermine US interests." The move did not represent an indefinite US commitment, the US said, urging Somalia and the African Union to accelerate preparations for a transition towards more sustainable regional security arrangements. The decision marks a shift from Washington's position in July 2026, when it informed partners that it would no longer support UNSOS beyond the current AUSSOM authorization, which expires on 31 December 2026. The US had expressed frustration over limited progress against al-Shabaab , delays in Somalia assuming greater responsibility for its security, and insufficient reforms. Follow us on WhatsApp | LinkedIn for the latest headlines In September, Washington softened its position, allowing for a proposed 12-month drawdown of UNSOS beginning in January 2027, followed by the liquidation of the mission. UNSOS provides essential logistical support to AUSSOM, including fuel, food rations, medical services and transportation. The support is considered critical to sustaining the approximately 12,000-strong AU force conducting operations against al-Shabaab. The mission's 2026/27 budget stands at approximately $481 million. The US has contributed nearly $2 billion in assessed contributions to UNSOS and its predecessors since 2007, in addition to more than $1.6 billion in bilateral assistance supporting African troop-contributing countries. Somalia's Ministry of Defence welcomed Washington's latest decision in a statement issued on 16 November, describing the US as the country's "largest and most steadfast partner in countering Al-Shabaab" and saying the move reaffirmed an "enduring partnership." The ministry said US assistance had helped strengthen Somali security institutions, sustain international operations and protect gains made against al-Shabaab. It added that the renewal would "preserve operational continuity, protect recent gains, and enable Somali forces to expand security across liberated areas." It reiterated the government's intention to assume primary responsibility for national security "in the near future" and called on international partners to "share the burden and sustain support for Somalia's security transition." Somalia continues to face significant security and political challenges as Al-Shabaab retains control over substantial areas and continues to pose a major threat. Somalia's Internal political tensions are also complicating the country's security transition. Furthermore, Uganda, AUSSOM's largest troop-contributing country, has indicated plans to withdraw its forces fully by the end of 2027. ethiopia.title: OLA Disputes Rights Commission Findings On Arsi Killings, Accuses Commission of Political Bias
ethiopia.content: Ethiopia: OLA Disputes Rights Commission Findings On Arsi Killings, Accuses Commission of Political Bias - allAfrica.com AllAfrica English (current) En Français Toggle navigation My Account Toggle navigation AllAfrica My Account English (current) En Français Ethiopia: OLA Disputes Rights Commission Findings On Arsi Killings, Accuses Commission of Political Bias 17 November 2026 Addis Standard (Addis Ababa) Addis Abeba — The Oromo Liberation Army (OLA) has disputed the Ethiopian Human Rights Commission's (EHRC) findings on deadly October attacks in Arsi woreda of southeast Oromia Zone, accusing the commission of being structurally compromised and questioning its decision to investigate the area while other civilian attacks across the country remain unaddressed. In a statement issued on November 16, the OLA High Command said its investigation into the violence in Shirka District found that "multiple armed actors", including Ethiopian National Defense Force (ENDF) personnel, counter-insurgency forces, state militia and armed Amhara civilians, were operating in the area. The group alleged that on October 18, an Oromo woman returning from a marketplace was shot dead by an armed civilian. OLA fighters subsequently attacked what it described as an encampment of these armed individuals in Birboof Collee, Shirkaa District. Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn The group acknowledged that the ensuing confrontation "regrettably led to civilian deaths," but disputed the characterization of those killed as ordinary civilians, claiming they were "part-time combatants" mobilized by government forces. The OLA's response follows the EHRC's November 3 report on the violence in Shirka, as well as a series of deadly attacks in the wider Arsi area that have raised concerns over civilian protection and the proliferation of armed groups. Addis Standard reported that on October 24 and 25, armed attackers killed at least 48 civilians and severely injured more than 31 others in attacks on Chole and Birbo kebeles of Shirka Woreda. Witnesses described attackers moving door-to-door, shooting and stabbing residents, looting property and using heavy weapons during an assault lasting nearly six hours. The victims included women, elderly people and at least six children. The Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church's Holy Synod separately reported that 46 Orthodox faithful were killed across Tereta, Chole and Birbo kebeles on October 24, in addition to 14 people killed in nearby Merti Woreda on October 20. The violence was followed by mass arrests. On October 28, Addis Standard reported that residents had raised concerns over the detention of more than 50 people, allegedly for participating in mass burials, attending funerals or helping transport and treat wounded victims. On November 2, the Oromia regional government announced that 73 individuals had been taken into custody in connection with the killings, describing the arrests as part of "security operations targeting OLF-Shane" and other groups it says are considered to be security threats. Authorities claimed stability had been restored in six kebeles. The OLA's November 16 statement challenged the credibility and impartiality of the EHRC's investigation, questioning why the commission had singled out Arsi while other areas experiencing civilian attacks had received less attention. "In a country experiencing daily attacks on civilians across multiple fronts of a protracted civil war, why single out Arsi for investigation?" the group asked, adding, "Why have ongoing attacks, such as the one in Moyale, attracted zero attention from the Commission?" It also questioned the commission's reliance on information from government institutions without adequately acknowledging what it described as their inherent conflict of interest. "The EHRC is an extension of the regime and operates within a political order whose security forces stand accused of perpetrating the very abuses it is supposed to investigate," the statement said. The group further questioned whether the commission could meaningfully hold authorities accountable while operating within the same political and institutional structures it is mandated to scrutinize. The group further questioned whether the commission could meaningfully hold authorities accountable while operating within the same political and institutional structures it is mandated to scrutinize. Beyond the immediate violence, the OLA framed the Arsi attacks as part of what it described as Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed's deliberate strategy of exploiting ethnic and religious divisions to prevent opposition groups and communities from forming a common front against his government. The group warned that the approach was pushing Ethiopia towards a breaking point, with consequences extending beyond its borders and potentially worsening instability across the Horn of Africa. "It is a governing strategy that turns communities against one another, institutions into instruments of political convenience, and national crisis into a source of regional insecurity." ethiopia.summary: The Oromo Liberation Army (OLA) has rejected the findings of the Ethiopian Human Rights Commission (EHRC) regarding the violent attacks in Arsi woreda, which occurred in October. The OLA accused the EHRC of political bias and questioned its decision to focus on Arsi while ignoring other civilian attacks across Ethiopia. In a statement, the OLA claimed that multiple armed groups, including government forces, were involved in the violence, which resulted in civilian casualties. They argued that those killed were not ordinary civilians but "part-time combatants" aligned with government forces. The OLA criticized the EHRC for relying on government information, suggesting it undermines the commission's credibility. They also framed the violence as part of Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed's strategy to exploit ethnic divisions, warning that this approach could lead to greater instability in Ethiopia and the Horn of Africa. The OLA's statement reflects broader concerns about the ongoing civil conflict and the role of government institutions in perpetuating violence.

ethiopia.title: Ethiopia's Role Indispensable to Red Sea Security, Says Strategic Forum CEO
ethiopia.content: Ethiopia's Role Indispensable to Red Sea Security, Says Strategic Forum CEO - allAfrica.com AllAfrica English (current) En Français Toggle navigation My Account Toggle navigation AllAfrica My Account English (current) En Français Ethiopia's Role Indispensable to Red Sea Security, Says Strategic Forum CEO 17 November 2026 Ethiopian News Agency (Addis Ababa) Addis Ababa — Ethiopia's strategic importance to Red Sea security is growing amid shifting geopolitical dynamics and intensifying military competition in the Horn of Africa, Founder and CEO of the newly established Nile and Red Sea Strategic Forum, Solomon Tefera said. Speaking to ENA, Solomon argued that lasting security and stability in the Red Sea region cannot be achieved without Ethiopia's meaningful participation, given its strategic geographical position, population of approximately 130 million and far-reaching economic and security interests. "Previously, it was Ethiopia that needed the Red Sea. Now, the Red Sea itself needs Ethiopia," he said. Solomon further underscored the country's potential role in safeguarding regional maritime security. Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn He noted that the Horn of Africa has increasingly become a focal point of geopolitical and military competition, with several foreign powers maintaining military bases and security deployments across the region. This evolving security landscape, he argued, makes Ethiopia an essential stakeholder in regional maritime security arrangements. For Ethiopia, the stakes are particularly high. As a landlocked country heavily dependent on Djibouti's port for its international trade, the country remains exposed to potential disruptions along critical maritime corridors, especially the Bab-el-Mandeb Strait, Solomon explained. Although alternative shipping routes exist, instability or interruptions around this strategic chokepoint could significantly affect Ethiopia's access to international markets and the movement of essential imports. He stressed that the implications extend well beyond trade, as disruptions to maritime supply chains could affect the availability of critical commodities, including fuel, fertilizers and military equipment, while placing additional pressure on the national economy and foreign currency resources. Against this backdrop, Solomon described reliable maritime access as a strategic imperative closely linked to Ethiopia's economic resilience, national security and long-term development ambitions. "Access to the sea is an existential issue for Ethiopia, not a matter of luxury," he emphasized. With a population of around 130 million and expanding economic ambitions, Ethiopia's maritime interests should be viewed not merely as a national concern but also within the broader context of regional economic integration and shared prosperity, he added. Citing the Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam (GERD), he noted that the flagship project illustrates how Ethiopia's development ambitions can contribute to wider regional interests, including those of neighboring countries such as Djibouti and Kenya. He said a similar approach to maritime engagement could open new avenues for regional economic cooperation, connectivity and shared prosperity. The Forum CEO also called for greater international and academic attention to the historical, geographical and legal dimensions of Ethiopia's loss of direct sea access, arguing that these issues warrant informed discussion and a deeper understanding across the Horn of Africa. He emphasized that examining Ethiopia's maritime interests within their historical and legal context could help foster constructive dialogue, mutual understanding and practical cooperation among countries in the region. ethiopia.title: Conflicts, Economic Uncertainty and Climate Pressures Dominate International Agenda
ethiopia.content: Ethiopia: Conflicts, Economic Uncertainty and Climate Pressures Dominate International Agenda - allAfrica.com AllAfrica English (current) En Français Toggle navigation My Account Toggle navigation AllAfrica My Account English (current) En Français Ethiopia: Conflicts, Economic Uncertainty and Climate Pressures Dominate International Agenda 16 November 2026 Ethiopian News Agency (Addis Ababa) The week of November 9-15, 2026, underscored the growing complexity of the international landscape, as geopolitical tensions, economic uncertainty, humanitarian emergencies and climate challenges continued to shape global affairs. Developments across the Middle East, Eastern Europe and Southeast Asia highlighted how conflicts, economic pressures and environmental risks increasingly transcend national borders, reinforcing the need for stronger international cooperation and coordinated responses. From persistent security tensions and shifting trade dynamics to climate negotiations and emerging technological risks, the week's developments reflected an international system facing multiple, interconnected challenges. Regional Conflicts and International Stability Geopolitical tensions remained a major concern for international peace and security, with the wars in Ukraine and the Middle East continuing to command global attention. Follow us on WhatsApp | LinkedIn for the latest headlines In Ukraine, continued attacks on electricity infrastructure heightened concerns over civilian access to heating, electricity and other essential services as winter approached. The situation underscored the vulnerability of critical infrastructure during armed conflict and the broader humanitarian consequences of prolonged hostilities. Meanwhile, tensions involving Iran and the wider Middle East continued to carry implications for regional security and global energy markets. The strategic importance of the Strait of Hormuz, through which a substantial share of internationally traded oil passes, made the potential disruption of maritime transportation a persistent concern for energy-importing economies. In Southeast Asia, the ASEAN Summit in Manila placed regional security and Myanmar's prolonged political crisis high on the diplomatic agenda. Discussions also addressed tensions in the South China Sea, where competing territorial claims and strategic interests continued to test regional cooperation. Despite diplomatic initiatives, differences over political legitimacy, sovereignty and security remained significant obstacles to lasting stability. Global Economic Developments The global economy continued to navigate a challenging environment shaped by inflationary pressures, monetary policy uncertainty and shifting international trade patterns. In the United States, persistent inflation complicated expectations surrounding Federal Reserve monetary policy. The prospect of interest rates remaining elevated raised concerns about international borrowing costs, investment flows and financial conditions, particularly for developing economies already facing debt and financing pressures. China, meanwhile, recorded strong trade performance in October. According to the International Monetary Fund's November 10 Global Markets Monitor, exports increased by 35.2 percent year-on-year, while imports rose by 41.6 percent. High-technology exports expanded by 66.6 percent, highlighting the growing importance of advanced manufacturing in China's global trade position. The country's year-to-date trade surplus also exceeded one trillion US dollars, underscoring its continued influence on international commerce and global supply chains. Meanwhile, oil prices faced downward pressure amid expectations of diplomatic progress in the Middle East. Nevertheless, the possibility of disruptions to shipping through the Strait of Hormuz continued to expose the global economy to energy-supply risks, demonstrating the close relationship between geopolitical developments and economic stability. Climate Diplomacy and COP31 Climate change remained a major international priority, with the 31st United Nations Climate Change Conference (COP31), held in Antalya, Türkiye, providing a central platform for negotiations on emissions reduction, climate finance, renewable energy and adaptation. Developing countries, particularly African nations and vulnerable island states, renewed calls for predictable and accessible climate financing, technology transfer and stronger international support to address the growing impacts of climate change. On November 14, UN Climate Change Executive Secretary Simon Stiell urged negotiators to accelerate discussions, warning that wars, inflation and competing international crises risked pushing climate action down governments' political priorities. The conference also highlighted the persistent gap between existing national climate commitments and the measures required to keep the global temperature increase within the 1.5-degree Celsius threshold. Among the initiatives discussed were Türkiye's global electrification proposal and efforts to mobilize more than one billion US dollars for resilience programmes benefiting 14 island economies. For Africa, COP31 represented an important opportunity to advance priorities extending beyond emissions reduction to include climate justice, adaptation financing, renewable energy development, sustainable agriculture and forest conservation. The continent's position remained particularly important given its limited contribution to historical global emissions and disproportionate exposure to climate-related risks. Democracy, Governance and Regional Cooperation Democratic governance and regional political stability remained central to discussions in Southeast Asia, particularly amid the prolonged crisis in Myanmar. At the ASEAN Summit, the limited progress in implementing the bloc's five-point peace framework highlighted the difficulties regional institutions face in addressing protracted political conflicts. The situation continued to raise questions about the effectiveness of regional diplomatic mechanisms in promoting political dialogue, reconciliation and stability. At the same time, tensions in the South China Sea demonstrated the importance of sustained diplomatic engagement and regional cooperation in managing competing territorial and maritime interests. These developments reinforced the need for effective multilateral institutions capable of addressing political disagreements while safeguarding regional peace, sovereignty and international law. Humanitarian Emergencies and Civilian Protection Humanitarian emergencies continued to deepen the vulnerability of populations affected by conflict and extreme weather. In Gaza, heavy rainfall damaged temporary shelters and essential infrastructure, worsening already difficult living conditions for displaced families. A UN humanitarian situation report issued on November 13 indicated that more than 46,000 households had been affected by flooding and shelter damage, underscoring the urgent need for humanitarian assistance and improved protection for vulnerable communities. In Ukraine, continued attacks on electricity infrastructure threatened access to heating, healthcare, water and other essential services as temperatures declined. Together, these developments illustrated how armed conflict and extreme weather can compound humanitarian crises, particularly where infrastructure has already been weakened and populations have limited access to basic necessities. They reinforced the importance of sustained humanitarian access, civilian protection and international assistance in accordance with international humanitarian law. Technology, Artificial Intelligence and International Security The rapid advancement of emerging technologies, particularly artificial intelligence and autonomous weapons systems, added another important dimension to international security discussions. The United Nations Convention on Certain Conventional Weapons was preparing for its Seventh Review Conference in Geneva, scheduled for November 16-20. Governments were expected to consider further steps toward developing international rules governing autonomous weapons systems. Growing concerns over accountability, civilian protection and compliance with international humanitarian law have intensified as artificial intelligence becomes increasingly integrated into military operations and weapons technologies. Beyond security applications, AI is also reshaping economic competitiveness, public administration, scientific research and international trade. Its expanding influence presents both opportunities and challenges, particularly for developing countries seeking to participate in the emerging digital economy. For these countries, investment in digital infrastructure, education, research, skills development and local innovation will be essential to narrowing technological gaps and ensuring that the benefits of digital transformation are more widely shared. Africa and the Global South: Shared Challenges, Common Priorities The week's international developments further highlighted the interconnected challenges confronting Africa and the wider Global South, including mounting debt pressures, climate vulnerability, food insecurity, infrastructure financing gaps and unequal access to international markets. For African economies, strengthening regional integration, expanding productive capacity and improving transport and energy infrastructure remain essential to achieving sustainable growth and greater economic resilience. The African Continental Free Trade Area (AfCFTA) offers a significant opportunity to expand intra-African trade, strengthen industrial cooperation and create a more integrated continental market. However, realizing its full potential will require continued investment in infrastructure, efficient customs systems, trade facilitation and domestic productive capacity. Climate finance also remained a critical priority. COP31 provided African countries with an important platform to press for more accessible financing, technology transfer and international partnerships to support renewable energy, agricultural modernization, forest conservation and climate adaptation. Beyond these immediate priorities, the broader challenge for the Global South is to secure a more equitable role in international economic and political decision-making, ensuring that global responses to shared challenges reflect the interests and development needs of all countries. Conclusion: The Case for Stronger Global Cooperation The developments of November 9-15 demonstrated that international security, economic stability, humanitarian protection, climate action and technological advancement are increasingly interconnected. Continuing conflicts in Ukraine and the Middle East highlighted the urgent need for sustained diplomatic engagement and civilian protection. Economic developments in the United States and China illustrated how the policies and performance of major economies influence global trade, financial conditions and developing countries. Meanwhile, COP31 brought renewed attention to the unresolved questions of climate responsibility and financing, while discussions on autonomous weapons underscored the growing importance of international technology governance. Taken together, the week's developments point to a central challenge facing the international community: addressing global crises not as isolated events, but as interconnected problems requiring coordinated and forward-looking solutions. Strengthening multilateral institutions, revitalizing diplomatic mechanisms, promoting inclusive economic growth and ensuring equitable access to climate finance and emerging technologies will be essential to building a more stable, resilient and sustainable international order. Conflicts in Ukraine and the Middle East continued to dominate global discussions, with concerns over humanitarian impacts and energy security. The ASEAN Summit addressed regional stability issues, particularly regarding Myanmar and territorial disputes in the South China Sea. Economically, inflation and shifting trade patterns posed challenges, particularly for developing nations. Meanwhile, COP31 emphasized the urgent need for climate action, with developing countries advocating for accessible financing and technology transfer. Humanitarian crises, exacerbated by conflict and extreme weather, underscored the necessity for international assistance. Additionally, advancements in technology, particularly artificial intelligence, raised new security concerns, prompting discussions on governance. Overall, the interconnected nature of these issues calls for enhanced global cooperation to effectively address the multifaceted challenges facing the international community.

somalia.title: Somalia: Waagacusub Investigation Uncovers Alleged Laftagareen–Al-Shabaab Cooperation - Sunatimes.com
somalia.content: Somalia: Waagacusub Investigation Uncovers Alleged Laftagareen–Al-Shabaab Cooperation Home About Us Quran Investigative Reports Latest News Featured Items Articles Contact Us ALSO IN THE NEWS Somalia: Waagacusub Investigation Uncovers Alleged Laftagareen–Al-Shabaab Cooperation 0 Wednesday November 18, 2026 - 04:27:22 in Latest News by Super Admin Visits: 139 (Rating 0.0/5 Stars) Total Votes: 0 0 0 Share via Social Media Somalia: Waagacusub Investigation Uncovers Alleged Laftagareen–Al-Shabaab Cooperation Waagacusub Investigation Raises Serious Allegations of Cooperation Between Laftagareen-Aligned Forces, Al-Shabaab and Ethiopian Troops Share Waagacusub Investigation Raises Serious Allegations of Cooperation Between Laftagareen-Aligned Forces, Al-Shabaab and Ethiopian Troops Independent investigation reports alleged coordination, shared resources and military cooperation in Somalia's South West State, particularly around Diinsoor. MOGADISHU, Somalia — Waagacusub Media | Special Investigative Report An independent investigation conducted by Waagacusub Media journalists has uncovered allegations of cooperation between armed forces loyal to Abdiaziz Hassan Mohamed, widely known as Abdiaziz Laftagareen, and militants belonging to the Al-Qaeda-linked terrorist organization Al-Shabaab. According to findings reported by Waagacusub's investigative team, forces aligned with Laftagareen and Al-Shabaab fighters have allegedly operated in close proximity, shared access to essential resources and coordinated military activities in parts of Somalia's South West State. The investigation also raises serious questions about reported encounters between Ethiopian military personnel and Al-Shabaab fighters in the Diinsoor area. Allegations of a Secret Agreement Waagacusub's investigation raises allegations that Laftagareen reached an understanding with Al-Shabaab involving territorial control, military operations and the administration of areas captured during armed offensives. According to information gathered by the investigative team, forces loyal to Laftagareen and Al-Shabaab fighters allegedly participated in coordinated operations against selected locations. Under the reported arrangement, Laftagareen-aligned forces would be permitted to publicly claim responsibility for capturing territory, while Al-Shabaab would allegedly retain influence over its administration and control. If substantiated, such an arrangement would raise serious concerns about the integrity of counterterrorism operations, the security of civilian populations and the relationship between armed groups operating in South West State. The precise terms, participants and authorization of any alleged agreement have not been independently established outside Waagacusub's reported investigation. Witnesses Describe Fighters Sharing Water and Food Local pastoralists interviewed by Waagacusub journalists described encounters in which they said fighters associated with different armed groups appeared to interact without hostility. According to these witnesses, individuals identified as Laftagareen-aligned troops and Al-Shabaab fighters were observed collecting water from the same wells, sharing food and moving through the same locations. The witnesses described these encounters as unusual given the publicly stated hostility between government-aligned forces and Al-Shabaab. Their accounts form part of Waagacusub's investigation into possible informal arrangements, local cooperation and the movement of armed personnel in contested areas. However, the reported observations do not, by themselves, establish a formal command relationship or prove the existence of an authorized military alliance. Ethiopian Troops and Al-Shabaab: Allegations from Diinsoor One of the investigation's most sensitive findings concerns reported interactions between Ethiopian military personnel and suspected Al-Shabaab fighters in the Diinsoor area. Local sources told Waagacusub that Ethiopian soldiers and individuals they identified as Al-Shabaab fighters were observed accessing the same water source. In a separate reported incident, witnesses alleged that Al-Shabaab members assisted Ethiopian troops whose military vehicle had become stuck in sand. According to these accounts, the vehicle was freed with assistance from individuals identified by local witnesses as Al-Shabaab fighters. If accurately documented, the incident would raise significant questions about the circumstances of the encounter and whether it reflected an isolated local interaction, a temporary arrangement or a broader pattern of cooperation. Waagacusub's reported findings do not, on the information presented here, establish that Ethiopian military commanders authorized cooperation with Al-Shabaab. Alleged Joint Operations and Territorial Control The investigation further raises allegations that Laftagareen-aligned forces and Al-Shabaab fighters have participated in coordinated attacks and territorial operations. Sources cited by Waagacusub described a purported arrangement under which one side could publicly announce military victories while the other maintained influence over local administration. Such allegations, if supported by corroborating operational evidence, would carry substantial implications for civilian protection, military accountability and counterterrorism efforts. Determining whether these reported incidents reflect coordinated command decisions would require examination of operational records, independently authenticated imagery, communications and testimony from individuals directly involved. Serious Questions for Regional Security The allegations reported by Waagacusub concern three distinct groups: Armed forces aligned with Abdiaziz Laftagareen. Militants belonging to Al-Shabaab. Ethiopian military personnel operating in Somalia. The investigation raises questions about whether reported interactions among these groups were isolated incidents, locally negotiated arrangements or evidence of more extensive cooperation. Any verified operational collaboration with Al-Shabaab would represent a matter of serious public interest and warrant examination by the relevant Somali and Ethiopian authorities. Accountability and the Right of Reply The findings reported by Waagacusub concern serious allegations against identifiable political and military actors. A complete assessment requires responses from Abdiaziz Laftagareen or his representatives, the relevant Ethiopian military authorities and other institutions responsible for security operations in the affected areas. Their responses should be incorporated into the investigation when obtained. Conclusion Waagacusub Media's independent investigation raises significant concerns about alleged cooperation, shared resources and coordinated military activity involving Laftagareen-aligned forces, Al-Shabaab fighters and Ethiopian troops in Somalia's South West State. The testimony gathered from local residents, particularly around Diinsoor, warrants careful scrutiny and further documentation. The central question is whether the reported encounters reflect isolated incidents or a broader arrangement involving military coordination and territorial control. Waagacusub Media will continue examining the reported incidents and seeking accountability from the individuals and institutions concerned. The report claims that these groups have coordinated military operations, shared resources, and interacted without hostility, raising serious concerns about the integrity of counterterrorism efforts. Local witnesses reported seeing Laftagareen-aligned troops and Al-Shabaab fighters sharing food and water, suggesting possible informal arrangements. If substantiated, these findings could indicate a broader pattern of collaboration that undermines regional security and civilian protection. The investigation calls for accountability from the involved parties and further scrutiny of the reported incidents to determine the nature and extent of these alleged alliances.

REUTERS/Stephanie Lecocq/File Photo SHARE Facebook X Pinterest WhatsApp Mogadishi (Somalia Today) — Two companies that guard the European Union’s civilian mission in Somalia have challenged the award of a four-year security contract to Sweden’s Vesper Group and its partners, Intelligence Online reported . Canada’s GardaWorld and France’s Amarante International lodged separate challenges, the publication said. Their contract expires on 30 November. Vesper said in October it would take over on 1 December . “ We are incredibly proud and humble to be awarded the contract to safeguard EUCAP, which plays a vital role in strengthening both regional and global security,” says Richard Möller CEO of Vesper Group. It remains unclear whether the challenges will affect the handover. The EU Capacity Building Mission in Somalia, known as EUCAP Somalia, selected the consortium on 1 October and concluded the contract on 14 October, according to its award notice . Vesper’s partners are Mogadishu-based Janus Global Operations Somalia and Hargeisa-based Risk Consultancy Global. The notice, published on 20 October, names EUCAP as the body responsible for procurement reviews. It records three complainants and one review request over allegedly discriminatory tender terms, without naming the complainants or giving an outcome. Price and drone defences EUCAP estimated the deal at 28 million euros. The consortium bid 23.66 million euros, and the award notice put the contract ceiling at 24.26 million euros. Unsuccessful bidders questioned whether the winning proposal offered adequate defences against drones, Intelligence Online reported, citing unnamed sources. One bidder doubted the price would cover the cost of deploying dozens of expatriate guards the job would require, the publication said. The publication said EUCAP, Vesper and Janus had not replied to its requests for comment. UN sanctions monitors said in a February report that member states had noted a “notable increase” in Al-Shabaab’s use of drones for surveillance. The group had also sought drone motors, frames and flight controllers, the monitors said. The mission received 12 requests to take part and eight bids, six of which it deemed inadmissible. Quality counted for 60 per cent of the assessment and price for 40 per cent. The notice said only shortlisted bidders would receive the detailed requirements. EUCAP told prospective bidders in June that consortia could include firms from outside the EU. Bidders relying on another company’s resources had to demonstrate they would have access to those resources for the work. The guidance followed questions about operating and firearms licences held by locally registered branches. Armed escorts The contract extends beyond Mogadishu to include Puntland and Somaliland, the award notice says. The EU’s foreign service rates the security risk as critical. The mission requires armed escorts whenever staff, official visitors and consultants travel in its areas of operation. The escort service “cannot be interrupted”, EUCAP said in its tender notice , warning that a gap in protection would delay its work. EUCAP advises, trains and equips Somalia’s federal police and helps the country enforce maritime law. The EU Council has extended the mission’s mandate until 28 February 2027 . In October, EUCAP said it had trained Puntland maritime police commanders in search-and-rescue at sea. Later that month, it hosted talks with Somalia’s internal security minister on police legislation and oversight of the security sector. The previous tender drew a challenge from Malta-based Geos Atlas after EUCAP rejected its consortium’s bid in 2024. The mission said the group lacked licences and firearms permits covering Puntland and Somaliland. The EU’s General Court dismissed the case in September 2025 , finding that the consortium had failed to meet the firearms permit requirement. The tender rules allowed bidders to show in writing that they would obtain the permits by the time of the award. Amarante won that tender, Intelligence Online reported. Ahmed Ali Sheikh Ahmed Ali Sheikh is the founder and Editor-in-Chief of Somalia Today and also founded Caasimada Online. A former VOA journalist and McClatchy stringer, he has over 15 years’ experience covering politics, security and society. somalia.summary: Two companies, Canada’s GardaWorld and France’s Amarante International, have formally challenged the awarding of a €24 million security contract to Sweden’s Vesper Group for the European Union’s civilian mission in Somalia, according to a report by Intelligence Online. The contract, which is set to begin on December 1, follows the expiration of the current contract on November 30. Vesper Group, along with its partners Janus Global Operations Somalia and Risk Consultancy Global, was selected by the EU Capacity Building Mission in Somalia (EUCAP) on October 1. The challengers have raised concerns regarding the adequacy of the winning bid's drone defenses and whether the proposed budget can support the deployment of necessary expatriate guards. The EU’s foreign service has classified the security risk in Somalia as critical, necessitating armed escorts for mission personnel. The EU has extended the mission's mandate until February 28, 2027, emphasizing its role in training and equipping Somalia’s federal police.

somalia.title: Climate shocks, insecurity drive displacement in Somalia: UN - Xinhua
somalia.content: Climate shocks, insecurity drive displacement in Somalia: UN-Xinhua Climate shocks, insecurity drive displacement in Somalia: UN Source: Xinhua Editor: huaxia 2026-11-18 06:23:15 This photo taken on Jan. 11, 2026 shows the damaged Mogadishu Lighthouse in Mogadishu, Somalia. (Xinhua/Yan Yujing) UNITED NATIONS, Nov. 17 (Xinhua) -- Drought, flooding and violence continue to displace people and deepen humanitarian needs in Somalia, UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA) said Tuesday. More than 3.3 million people, most of them women, children and older people, are currently displaced across the country. Between January and September alone, more than 800,000 people were newly uprooted, 70 percent of them due to drought, OCHA said, citing figures from the UN Refugee Agency. Projected El Nino-related flooding could displace hundreds of thousands more people by December, it warned. Last month alone, floods displaced more than 17,500 people and affected over 170,000. Violence in Bay and Bari regions also uprooted some 9,500 people in September and October, said the office. "Displacement also puts people at greater risk of violence, exploitation and abuse, especially women and girls, children, people with disabilities and minority communities," it said. The International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC) said the Bay and Bakool regions in the federal state of South West are among the hardest-hit areas for food insecurity. Armed conflict, which has escalated since March, threatens to worsen conditions for communities still reeling from the effects of drought. "With widespread displacement, food shortages and limited access to health care due to aid cuts that have resulted in clinic closures, the anticipated rainfall could overwhelm families already struggling to cope," the ICRC said. Severe funding shortfalls are forcing cuts of assistance to the country, OCHA said, adding the number of people receiving food assistance fell from 1.1 million people in January to about 600,000 in June, mainly due to underfunding. Some 233 nutrition sites and 380 health facilities have also closed or reduced services this year due to funding shortfalls, it said, noting that the Somalia humanitarian response plan that requires 852 million U.S. dollars is just 36 percent funded. ■ Comments Comments (0) Send You may like Journalists work at media center for APEC Economic Leaders' Week in Shenzhen China's Sanya becomes popular winter destination for travelers Winter scenery of Sayram Lake in China's Xinjiang Documentary | Shenzhen: Beyond the Skyline Shenzhen embraces high-quality green development path Golden pomelo industry sweetens life in south China village More from GLOBALink APEC: Striving Together for Shared Prosperity U.S. scholar stresses APEC's crucial role in tackling transnational challenges China's 3rd APEC hosting comes amid push for opening-up's next frontier: APEC secretariat chief Follow us on More from GLOBALink APEC: Striving Together for Shared Prosperity U.S. scholar stresses APEC's crucial role in tackling transnational challenges China's 3rd APEC hosting comes amid push for opening-up's next frontier: APEC secretariat chief Follow us on Climate shocks, insecurity drive displacement in Somalia: UN
somalia.summary: Severe climate shocks and ongoing insecurity are driving significant displacement in Somalia, according to the UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA). Currently, over 3.3 million people, primarily women, children, and the elderly, are displaced across the country. From January to September 2026, more than 800,000 individuals were newly displaced, with 70% attributed to drought conditions. The situation is expected to worsen with projected El Niño-related flooding, which could displace hundreds of thousands more by December. Recent flooding has already affected over 170,000 people. Additionally, violence in the Bay and Bari regions has led to further displacements. The International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC) highlighted that armed conflict and food insecurity are exacerbating the humanitarian crisis, with funding shortfalls leading to reduced assistance and the closure of health facilities. The Somalia humanitarian response plan is severely underfunded, receiving only 36% of the required $852 million.

somalia.title: Cascades FC signs defender Brecc Evans and Somalia international Mo Mohamed - KMTR
somalia.content: Cascades FC signs defender Brecc Evans and Somalia international Mo Mohamed Skip to main content Close Download the App Get your news faster with our mobile experience Install News Weather Features Station Newsletter Sign Up Watch Live Now 47 ° Wed 51 ° Thu 47 ° Search Search User Icon Watch Cascades FC signs defender Brecc Evans and Somalia international Mo Mohamed by Sports Staff Tue, November 17, 2026 at 1:08 PM Updated Tue, November 17, 2026 at 4:27 PM (Image courtesy Cascades FC) Comment on this story 0 Comment Share story Share topics: Cascades Brecc Evans Mo Mohamed USL League One Somalia Eugene Defender Portland Hearts of Pine EUGENE, Ore. — Cascades FC is adding proven experience and international flair to its back line, signing veteran center back Brecc Evans and Oregon native Mo Mohamed, who recently debuted for the Somalia national team. The club announced the moves Tuesday, Nov. 17, 2026, in Eugene, Oregon. The signings are pending league and federation approval. Evans has been one of USL League One’s top defenders since turning pro in 2019, while Mohamed is an attacking fullback who earned attention this fall after his first appearances with Somalia. “We identified Brecc years ago and are very happy to get him on our side for the future here at Cascades FC,” head coach Darren Sawatzky said. “Brecc shined for North Texas in year one of our league and his stops along the way have proven that he brings a winning mentality into the locker room. We see Brecc as a leader with experience and he has a bite that is necessary to be successful in USL League One. “Momo has gotten better and better over the course of his USL League One time, and this has culminated in his call up to the Somalian national team. He is a fiery outside back with the ability to fly forward and create both from the flank areas and through the middle of the field. We are pumped to add another piece to both the defending core as well as the opportunity to attack teams in different ways.” Evans spent the 2026 season with Portland Hearts of Pine, anchoring the middle of the back line and making 32 appearances across all competitions. He scored one goal and ranked among the league leaders in several defensive categories, including 178 clearances, the second-most in USL League One. He also was the league’s fourth-most accurate long passer and won more than 60% of his aerial duels. In 2025 with FC Naples, Evans led USL League One with 223 clearances and ranked third with a plus-6.35 goals added mark. He added 71 recoveries and 21 interceptions and again won 60% of his duels, earning USL League One All-League Second Team honors. Evans played the 2022-24 seasons with Northern Colorado Hailstorm FC, helping the club win the inaugural Jägermeister Cup and finishing his stint as the team’s all-time leader in minutes played. Before that, he spent 2021 with Memphis 901 FC and helped the club reach the USL Championship playoffs for the first time in franchise history. A Culver City, California, native, Evans attended California Polytechnic State University in 2018 and earned Big West All-Freshman and All-Big West Third Team honors before turning professional. He signed with North Texas SC ahead of the 2019 season and, as a rookie, was named captain of a team that included future U.S. Men’s National Team standout Ricardo Pepi. North Texas won the league championship that year, with Evans ranking as the league’s third-most accurate passer. He later was loaned to Austin Bold for the COVID-shortened 2020 season. “I am really grateful for this opportunity and the belief shown in me by the club and the entire staff,” Evans said. “When first hearing about the chance to be a part of professional soccer in Eugene, I was thrilled. The time is now to give the community what they deserve. I am counting down the days until the home opener at Civic Park and am working hard daily to bring a trophy to the loyal fanbase of Sporting Cascades.” Mohamed, a Portland native, played at Cleveland High School before starring at Seattle University. He earned Second-Team All-WAC and WAC All-Tournament Team honors while helping lead Seattle University to the Western Athletic Conference title in 2024. He spent time with Portland Timbers 2 in early 2025 before signing with Maine’s Portland Hearts of Pine on a 25-day contract in late May. He scored in his first appearance in a 4-2 upset of USL Championship side Detroit City FC in the USL Jägermeister Cup, and the club soon converted his deal into a season-long contract. Mohamed went on to make 17 appearances for Hearts, including starts in both playoff matches. He played 77 minutes in a 1-0 quarterfinal win against Chattanooga Red Wolves and all 120 minutes in a semifinal against Spokane Velocity, which Spokane won on penalties. Eligible to represent Somalia through his mother’s side of the family, Mohamed was on the bench for Africa Cup of Nations qualifiers against Mauritius in March before making his debut against The Gambia in September. In his second international appearance, against Ivory Coast on Sept. 29, Mohamed was assigned to mark Yan Diomande, described by the club as a former Blue Crow Sports Group prodigy who earlier this year became the most expensive signing in Real Madrid history. “I’m grateful for the opportunity to be part of Cascades FC this upcoming season,” Mohamed said. “I look forward to meeting everyone, contributing on and off the pitch, and working towards building something special together.” Trending 65-year-old woman pinned under van after crash at Springfield intersection A 65-year-old woman suffered life-threatening injuries after she was struck by a vehicle and pinned underneath it Monday evening at a Springfield intersection, police said.Springfield police responded at 6:09 p.m. Nov. Evans, a veteran center back, has been a standout in USL League One since turning professional in 2019, known for his leadership and defensive skills. He had a successful 2026 season with Portland Hearts of Pine, making 32 appearances and ranking high in defensive statistics. Mohamed, an Oregon native, recently debuted for the Somalia national team and is recognized for his attacking abilities as a fullback. He gained attention during his time at Seattle University and made a significant impact with Portland Hearts of Pine. Both players are expected to enhance Cascades FC's defensive and attacking capabilities. Head coach Darren Sawatzky expressed enthusiasm about the signings, emphasizing their potential contributions to the team’s success in the upcoming season. The signings are pending approval from the league and federation.

somalia.title: Mohamud Accuses UAE of Funding Division and Building Parallel Forces in Televised Address - FTL Somalia
somalia.content: Mohamud Accuses UAE of Funding Division and Building Parallel Forces in Televised Address - Somali News today Live Home Politics Security Elections More News Premium Economy & Business Education Entertainment & Lifestyle Environment & Climate Health International Relations Technology & Innovation Sports News By Region Nationwide Benadir Galmudug Hirshabelle Jubaland Puntland South West State Somaliland North Eastern State Resources Infographics Downloads Videos FAQ About Somalia Generic selectors Exact matches only Search in title Search in content Post Type Selectors Home Politics Security Elections More News Premium Economy & Business Education Entertainment & Lifestyle Environment & Climate Health International Relations Technology & Innovation Sports News By Region Nationwide Benadir Galmudug Hirshabelle Jubaland Puntland South West State Somaliland North Eastern State Resources Infographics Downloads Videos FAQ About Somalia Generic selectors Exact matches only Search in title Search in content Post Type Selectors Generic selectors Exact matches only Search in title Search in content Post Type Selectors International Relations Nationwide Mohamud Accuses UAE of Funding Division and Building Parallel Forces in Televised Address November 17, 2026 6 min read MOGADISHU , President Hassan Sheikh Mohamud used a televised address to the nation on Monday to accuse the United Arab Emirates of years of interference in Somalia’s internal affairs, alleging that Abu Dhabi has funded political division, signed port deals outside federal authority, and helped establish parallel security structures that weaken the national army. The speech was the most direct and detailed public case the President has made against the UAE since his government annulled all bilateral agreements with Abu Dhabi in January 2026. It drew a line between what Mohamud described as the historic friendship between the Somali and Emirati peoples and what he characterized as a sustained campaign by the Emirati government to undermine Somali sovereignty and unity. The Ports and the Security Architecture At the center of the President’s address were the port agreements that the UAE has signed with regional administrations in Somaliland, Puntland, and Jubaland. Mohamud said the UAE had entered into deals relating to Berbera, Bosaso, and Kismayo with local authorities rather than the Federal Government, and argued that Somalia’s strategic infrastructure cannot be managed outside the constitutional order. The Berbera arrangement has been the most contentious. The UAE, through DP World, has invested heavily in the port and maintains a military presence at the adjacent airport. As detailed in the coverage of the Berbera base , satellite imagery and security sources have indicated that the facility is being developed for Emirati, Israeli, and American strategic use. Mohamud’s speech framed these arrangements as part of a broader pattern of external powers bypassing Mogadishu. The President also accused the UAE of helping to establish military bases and forces that are not fully within the national security command. Parallel security structures, he said, weaken the cohesion of the Somali forces at a time when the country is fighting Al-Shabaab . The reference to parallel forces echoes longstanding concerns about the UAE’s support for regional militias and its training of forces outside the federal chain of command. The Israeli Recognition and the Berbera Incident Mohamud directly linked the UAE to Israel’s recognition of Somaliland in December 2025, saying Abu Dhabi had played a role in the decision and had declined to sign Arab and Islamic statements condemning it. As detailed in the coverage of Israel’s embassy in Hargeisa , the recognition was immediately condemned by Mogadishu, the African Union, and the Arab League, but the UAE was notably absent from the statements of condemnation. The President also referenced an incident in Berbera in January 2026, alleging that the UAE had used Somali territory to move a militia leader fleeing Yemen without the consent of the Federal Government. “Somali territory is not a road to be crossed unlawfully, not a commodity to be bought, and not a place to be entered at will,” he said. The January Decision and the Unresolved Dispute Mohamud recounted that his government had not acted hastily. After years of trying to resolve the dispute through dialogue and diplomacy, he said, the Council of Ministers decided on January 12, 2026, to annul all agreements with the UAE, including those on security, defense, and the economy, and closed Somali airspace to Emirati military and cargo aircraft. Ten months later, the causes of the dispute have not gone away. The President said the UAE had given political and financial support to some regional administrations, fueling disputes between the Federal Government and other political actors. He pointed to Libya, Yemen, and Sudan as examples of what he described as the UAE’s role in conflict and division, and warned Somalis that their country could face a similar fate if political unity is not strengthened. The speech left the door open to reconciliation, but on terms that the UAE has not accepted. Mohamud said Somalia is ready for a relationship based on equality, respect, and full recognition of its territorial unity, but that it will not accept agreements or steps that undermine statehood. Critical Note The President’s address is a political statement, and it should be assessed as one. It lays out a case against the UAE that is detailed and specific, The allegation that the UAE helped establish parallel security structures, for instance, is consistent with longstanding reporting on Emirati support for regional forces, but the government has not published the evidence it says it has. The more significant problem is that the speech describes a foreign policy failure without acknowledging its own role in it. Somalia’s relationship with the UAE did not collapse solely because of Emirati interference. It collapsed because Mogadishu could not control the regional administrations that signed the port deals, could not prevent Israel’s recognition of Somaliland, and could not offer the UAE a partnership that was more attractive than the one it found in Hargeisa and Bosaso. The President’s framing of the dispute as a story of Somali sovereignty versus foreign meddling is understandable, but it obscures the domestic weaknesses that gave foreign actors their openings. The speech also comes at a moment when the government’s own legitimacy is contested. The Supreme Court has ruled that the President’s mandate expired, the Chief Justice he dismissed has been defended by UN human rights experts, and armed mobilisation in Hiiraan has drawn fighters away from the counter-insurgency campaign. A government that is fighting its own judiciary and its own clans may find that its warnings about foreign interference carry less weight than they would in a moment of political unity. For the Somali public, the most important question is not whether the UAE has interfered. It is whether the government’s response to that interference has made Somalia stronger or more isolated and weaker. The January decision to annul the agreements was a assertion of sovereignty. Ten months later, the port deals remain in place, the UAE’s regional partners remain aligned with Abu Dhabi, and the Federal Government’s authority over its own territory remains contested. The speech drew a line. It did not change the reality on the other side of it.
